925.title: Forgiving the gunman (1983)
925.hook: John Paul II visits in prison the man who shot him
925.howItsDone: Catholics who volunteer in prison ministry visit inmates, often bringing Communion and listening, and some point to John Paul II's visit to Ağca and to Jesus's words in Matthew 25 as their pattern.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solidarity: a shipyard gate, a round table, and a country changed. Your line was without violence.

Cameras catch the scene, but not the words. Two chairs pulled close in a small prison cell in Rome. One man in white, one in a prisoner's clothes. They lean in until their heads nearly touch, and they talk quietly for a long time. At one point the man in white holds the other man's hand. The prisoner is Mehmet Ali Ağca. Some time before, in Saint Peter's Square, in front of a crowd, he raised a pistol and shot the man now sitting beside him. The visitor is John Paul the Second.
screen: `A CELL IN ROME, TWO CHAIRS.` → `THEY TALK FOR A LONG TIME.` → `THE GUNMAN AND THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Four moments make this story. First, the square. John Paul was riding slowly through the crowd in an open car when shots rang out. He was badly wounded and rushed to a hospital, and for a time it wasn't clear he would live. The gunman was caught on the spot. Second, the hospital. Within days, still weak, the pope spoke to the world by radio from his bed. He asked people to pray for the brother who had shot him, whom he had sincerely forgiven. Not the gunman. The brother. Third, the cell. After his recovery he went to the prison himself. No letter, no bishop in his place. He sat down and talked with the man, and afterward said that what they talked about would remain a secret between them, and that he had spoken to him as a brother whom he had pardoned and who had his complete trust. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus names prison visits among the things done for him, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." Fourth, what forgiveness didn't do. Ağca stayed in prison for years after the visit. The pope didn't pretend the shooting was small or that justice didn't matter. Catholic teaching holds forgiveness and justice side by side: you can release a debt in your heart and still let the courts do their work. Two chairs, two men, a held hand, and words they kept between them.
screen: `SHOTS IN SAINT PETER'S SQUARE.` · `FROM A HOSPITAL BED: MY BROTHER.` · `HE WENT TO THE CELL.` · `FORGIVENESS AND JUSTICE, BOTH.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something you can hold today, and picture them in a chair close to yours. You don't have to say it's fine: you can name what happened, and if you're ready, say I forgive you; if you're not, leave the chair there for another day. Forgiving never means putting yourself in harm's way. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, as the pope did.
Forgiving the gunman. John Paul the Second, shot in Saint Peter's Square, forgave Mehmet Ali Ağca and went to visit him in prison.
Your line: he went to the cell. Forgiveness walked in, and justice stayed. Day nine hundred twenty-five, complete.

926.title: Assisi, 1986
926.hook: leaders of many religions gather in Francis's town to pray for peace, each in their own way
926.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses and the Sant'Egidio community hold interreligious prayers for peace in the spirit of Assisi, where each tradition prays in its own way and the others listen in respectful silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving the gunman: two chairs in a Roman prison. Your line was he went to the cell.

Saffron, black, white, red: robes of every color fill the streets of a hill town in Italy, the town of Saint Francis. A Buddhist monk walks near an Orthodox bishop. Rabbis, Muslim leaders, Hindu teachers, Sikhs, Anglican and Lutheran church leaders, and leaders of traditional African and Native American religions have come, because the pope invited them, to pray for peace. But they won't say one prayer together. Each group goes to its own place to pray its own way. Then they come back to one square and stand side by side. This is Assisi.
screen: `A HILL TOWN FULL OF ROBES.` → `INVITED BY THE POPE.` → `TO PRAY FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: John Paul the Second called it a World Day of Prayer for Peace, and it worked in four steps. First, the invitation. He asked the leaders of the world's religions to come to Assisi, the town of Francis, a saint remembered for peace and for meeting a sultan in a time of war. He asked them to fast and pray, and asked nobody to give up anything they believed. Second, apart. Each tradition went to its own church, hall or open space and prayed in its own words and its own way. Catholics didn't lead the others' prayers; nobody was asked to join anyone else's worship. Third, together. In the afternoon they gathered in front of the basilica of Saint Francis, and one tradition after another offered its prayer for peace aloud while everyone else stood and listened in silence. As the pope put it, they weren't going to pray together, but they were together in order to pray. Fourth, the worry and the answer. Some Catholics were uneasy, afraid it would look as if all religions were being blended into one. The pope answered that this was exactly what wasn't happening: each prayed as itself, with respect, and none pretended the differences away. Later popes have gone back to Assisi in the same spirit. Jesus says in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." At Assisi, peacemaking began with something modest: standing still while your neighbor prays.
screen: `AN INVITATION TO FAST AND PRAY.` · `APART: EACH PRAYS IN ITS OWN WAY.` · `TOGETHER: STANDING IN SILENCE.` · `NOT BLENDED, NOT PRETENDING.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Think of the people near you who pray differently, or not at all: a coworker who fasts in another season, a family down the street with a different holy day, a friend who keeps no tradition. Picture them in that square, praying their own way while you stand quietly beside them. If you pray, pray for peace between religions; if not, simply hold them in mind.

Your line: together, not blended. Respect left every prayer whole, side by side. See you tomorrow.

927.title: World Youth Day
927.hook: a gathering of young Catholics, begun by John Paul II, where a pope meets the young of the world
927.howItsDone: Catholic parishes and dioceses send groups of young people to World Youth Day, often raising money together for the trip, and those who stay home sometimes gather locally on the same days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Assisi: many religions praying for peace, side by side. Your line was together, not blended.

A plain wooden cross is moving through an airport. Not a crucifix, just two beams, taller than the teenagers carrying it. They tip it to get it through the door, laughing, while a security guard holds the door open. It's on its way to a city where, in a few months, young Catholics from across the world will arrive with backpacks and flags, sleep on gym floors and in strangers' spare rooms, and sing in languages they don't speak. At the end they walk out to a field, spend the night under the open sky, and in the morning a pope says Mass for them. It's called World Youth Day, though it lasts most of a week.
screen: `A WOODEN CROSS AT THE AIRPORT.` → `BACKPACKS, FLAGS, GYM FLOORS.` → `A NIGHT IN A FIELD.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. John Paul the Second, the pope of be not afraid, invited the young to Rome, and then kept inviting them, to a different city each time. Later popes kept the invitation going. It became a habit of the Church: every few years, the young gather. Second, the cross. John Paul gave a simple wooden cross to young people and asked them to carry it around the world. It travels from country to country before each gathering, through prisons, hospitals, schools and parishes, with an icon of Mary beside it. Third, the shape of the week: teaching from bishops in many languages, confession in tents and on folding chairs, music late into the night. Then the pilgrimage on foot to a big field, a night vigil with candles, and the closing Mass in the morning. The sleeping on the ground is part of it. Fourth, why the young. The prophet Joel promised a day when God's spirit would be poured out on everyone, and the Douay-Rheims gives his line: "your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions." And Paul writes to Timothy, a young church leader: "Let no man despise thy youth." In these texts the young aren't the Church's future, someday. They're part of it now, with visions of their own. Some come back changed. Some come back sunburned and tired and not sure what happened. The Church sends the invitation either way.

segments.voice: Choose one young person you know, a niece, a student, the teenager who bags your groceries, and picture them with a backpack, far from home, a little lost and a little excited. If you pray, pray for them by name, maybe with Paul's line, let no man despise thy youth; if not, wish them good company.
Pilgrimage. The walk on foot to a big field that is part of every World Youth Day, ending in a night vigil and a morning Mass with the pope.

928.title: The Day of Pardon (2000)
928.hook: in St Peter's, the pope publicly asks forgiveness for sins committed by Catholics through history
928.howItsDone: Catholics confess their own sins in the sacrament of penance and say the Confiteor, with its words through my fault, at the start of Mass; the Day of Pardon brought that language to the Church's own history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, World Youth Day: a cross on the move and a night in a field. Your line was the young gather.

A Sunday in Lent, in St Peter's Basilica, and a crucifix stands near an old pope. One after another, cardinals and bishops step forward, and each names a kind of wrong. Not wrongs done to the Church. Wrongs done by its own members. After each one there's silence, and then the pope speaks a prayer asking pardon, and the people answer. Before it ends, the pope goes to the crucifix and kisses it. He was John Paul the Second, frail by then. The Church remembers it as the Day of Pardon: a very old institution, under its own famous dome, saying out loud, we did this.
screen: `A CRUCIFIX IN ST PETER'S.` → `WRONGS DONE BY ITS OWN MEMBERS.` → `WE DID THIS.`

segments.voice: The prayers came in a set order. First, what was named: sins committed in the service of truth, divisions among Christians, sins against the people of Israel, wrongs against love, peace and the dignity of peoples and cultures, against women, against the poor and the unborn. Broad on purpose. Some listeners wanted more names and details; some thought it went too far. Both reactions were real. Second, who was asking. The Church teaches that the Church itself is holy, and also that its members sin. So the prayers were spoken for the sins of her sons and daughters, past and present. Theologians had worked on exactly that distinction in a document called Memory and Reconciliation. Third, the scripture underneath. The first letter of John says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." A Church that says that to each person in confession was saying it about itself. Fourth, the other half. In his homily that day the pope paired two things: we forgive, and we ask forgiveness. Catholics have an old phrase for owning a wrong, from the Confiteor, one of the prayers that can open Mass: through my fault. That day a whole Church said it about its own history. It didn't settle everything. An apology spoken in Rome is a beginning. What comes after it is the hard part, and some of that story comes tomorrow.

segments.voice: Recall something that went wrong between you and someone else, where the blame is shared. Don't add up their part; find your own piece and name it plainly to yourself, the way those bishops did, in one sentence with no excuses. If you pray, bring it to God, perhaps with the old words, through my fault; if not, hold it honestly, without punishing yourself.
Mea culpa. Through my fault, the old phrase from the Confiteor that the whole Church said about its own history on the Day of Pardon.
Your line: we ask forgiveness. And in the same breath: we forgive. That's day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: The abuse crisis
929.hook: clergy abuse and cover-ups hurt children; survivors come first
929.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses commonly have safeguarding offices and require background checks and training for clergy, staff and volunteers who work with children; some keep a day of prayer for survivors of abuse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Day of Pardon: mea culpa, a Church asking forgiveness. Your line was we ask forgiveness.

A note before we start. Today's lesson is about the abuse of children by clergy, and about leaders who covered it up. Nothing graphic is described. If this touches your own life, you can stop here, or come back to it another day, and it's worth reaching out to someone you trust or a local support line. For everyone else: this is part of the long story of the Church in our time, and leaving it out would be its own kind of cover-up. Children and vulnerable adults were harmed by priests and religious they had every reason to trust. And when some of them spoke, they were not believed, or they were paid to stay quiet, while abusers were moved to new places. Today's word is what the Church calls the work of making sure that never happens again.
screen: `A NOTE BEFORE WE START.` → `HARM, AND THEN A COVER-UP.` → `TODAY'S WORD: SAFEGUARDING.`

segments.voice: Four things, said carefully. First, the harm was double. The abuse itself, then what came after: survivors who told the truth and were doubted, families pressured into silence, abusers sent somewhere new. Public reports and investigations described this pattern. Second, who broke it open. Not, first of all, the Church's leaders. Survivors, who kept telling their stories, often for years; journalists and investigators who listened; lay people and some clergy who refused to look away. Third, what the Church's leaders have said. Pope Francis wrote to the whole Church admitting that the Church had not acted in time, and he quoted Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it." Catholics also hear a hard warning from Jesus: for anyone who leads one of these little ones astray, it would be better to be drowned in the sea with a millstone around the neck. Fourth, the word. Safeguarding means the plain, unglamorous rules that protect children and vulnerable adults now: background checks, training, never one adult alone with a child, clear ways to report, and reporting to civil authorities. Some dioceses and parishes now have a named safeguarding office. Survivors and their advocates say rules alone aren't enough without honesty and accountability, and that work isn't finished. Through all of it, one principle: survivors first. Not the reputation of an institution. Not the comfort of the people in charge. The people who were harmed.

segments.voice: You don't need to picture anything. Bring to mind the people, often unnamed, who were harmed as children and then not believed, and let them come first, not last. If you pray, pray for their healing in whatever words you have; if not, hold them with respect.

930.title: The Catechism (1992)
930.hook: a single summary of Catholic belief, written for the whole world
930.howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference in parish classes, adult formation and preparation for the sacraments, often citing it by paragraph number; shorter local catechisms and the Compendium draw on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard day: the abuse crisis, and the word safeguarding. Your line was survivors first.

If someone asked you what Catholics actually believe, where would you send them? For a long time the answer depended on where you lived: each country, sometimes each diocese, had its own little question-and-answer book, and children memorized them. Who made us? God made us. There had been a catechism for the whole Church once before, written after the Council of Trent for parish priests. Then the bishops of the world, meeting in Rome, asked for a new one: one book for the whole Church, setting out the faith in order. It took years of drafting, and the bishops were asked for their comments. The result is a thick book of numbered paragraphs, on parish shelves and on phones: the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
screen: `WHAT DO CATHOLICS BELIEVE?` → `A LITTLE BOOK FOR EACH PLACE.` → `ONE BOOK FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Open it and the plan is plain. First, the shape: four parts, and once you know them the whole book opens up. The faith professed: the Creed, line by line. The faith celebrated: the liturgy and the sacraments. The faith lived: the life in Christ, including the Ten Commandments. The faith prayed: prayer, ending with the Our Father, line by line. Second, the numbers. Every paragraph is numbered, and the book cross-references itself in the margins, so a paragraph about baptism points you to others about grace, the Church, water at Easter. People cite it by number, the way you'd cite a verse. Third, who it's for. John Paul the Second, in the document that introduced it, called it a sure norm for teaching the faith, meant first for bishops and teachers, then for anyone who wants to know what the Church believes. It was never meant to replace local catechisms, but to be the reference they draw on. Fourth, the sources. Open it almost anywhere and the paragraphs are stitched from Scripture, the councils, saints and early writers. Luke opens his Gospel by telling Theophilus why he wrote it, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." The Catechism sets out to do the same at the size of a whole Church: one summary, in order, so the faith can be known, not just guessed at.
screen: `FOUR PARTS: BELIEVE, WORSHIP, LIVE, PRAY.` · `NUMBERED PARAGRAPHS, CITED LIKE VERSES.` · `A SURE NORM FOR TEACHING.` · `STITCHED FROM SCRIPTURE AND SAINTS.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

The Catechism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church: one summary of the faith, in four parts, in numbered paragraphs, for the whole Church.

931.title: Benedict XVI (2005–2013)
931.hook: a quiet theologian whose first encyclical was God is love
931.howItsDone: Catholics read the first letter of John at Mass at various points in the year, and parishes and charities sometimes study Deus caritas est for its teaching that care for the poor belongs to the Church's own life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catechism: one book, four parts, numbered paragraphs. Your line was one summary.

A new pope's first encyclical is watched closely: his first long letter to the whole Church, read for a program. This one came from a man who had spent his life as a professor and then as the Vatican's guardian of doctrine. Some expected rules. Its Latin title was three words: Deus caritas est. God is love. It opens with a line from the first letter of John, and then does something some readers didn't expect from a strict theologian. It talks about eros, the love of desire, and agape, the love that gives itself away, and says the two belong together.
screen: `A FIRST LETTER, CLOSELY WATCHED.` → `SOME EXPECTED RULES.` → `DEUS CARITAS EST.`

segments.voice: His name was Joseph Ratzinger; as pope he took the name Benedict. First, the scholar. He was a theologian before he was a bishop, a writer of books, more at home at a desk than on a balcony. He had worked on yesterday's Catechism, and for a long time he guarded Catholic teaching in Rome, which earned him critics as well as admirers. Second, the name: Benedict, the monk of Nursia whose rule shaped monasteries across Europe, and Benedict the Fifteenth, a pope who pleaded for peace in a world war. Third, the letter. The first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, uses an older English word for love: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him." Charity there isn't a donation. It's the Latin caritas, love itself. Benedict starts there and turns practical: if God is love, the Church's care for the poor and the sick isn't a side activity. It belongs to what the Church is, as much as the sacraments and the preaching of the word. Fourth, the disagreement. Some remember a brilliant, gentle teacher. Others remember the strict guardian of doctrine, or a papacy troubled by scandal. Both are part of the record. But his first letter to the whole Church had a three-word title. And that ends the week: from forgiving the gunman, through Assisi, World Youth Day, the Day of Pardon, the abuse crisis and the Catechism, to a pope whose first word to the Church was love.
screen: `JOSEPH RATZINGER, THE SCHOLAR.` · `THE NAME OF A MONK AND A PEACE POPE.` · `GOD IS CHARITY: LOVE ITSELF.` · `ADMIRED AND CRITICIZED.` · then, large: `GOD IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Say the line slowly, in the old words: God is charity, and he that abideth in charity abideth in God. Then put a face on it, someone who loved you when nothing was in it for them, a neighbor, a friend, a stranger who helped, and stay with them a while. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, simply be grateful.
Benedict the Sixteenth. Joseph Ratzinger, a theologian who became pope and whose first encyclical was Deus caritas est: God is love.
